opus-5.5.text:
I think research is the glue, honestly. When you start something like AMI Labs, you're not just hiring people to execute a roadmap. You're trying to gather people who share a certain conviction about where intelligence should go: that language alone isn't the whole story, and that we need systems that understand the world, that can model it, predict it, and plan within it. That's a research question first. It's not a product spec.

What I've found is that a hard, open research problem attracts a particular kind of person. They're not coming for a safe answer. They're coming because the question is interesting and nobody has solved it yet. So the research agenda itself becomes the thing that brings people together. It gives everyone a common language, even if they come from very different backgrounds, like vision, robotics, representation learning, or theory.

There's also a cultural side. In academia I always cared a lot about openness, about students being able to argue with me, about ideas winning on their merits rather than on seniority. I want that at AMI too. Research only works if people feel safe saying "I think this is wrong" or trying something weird that might fail for six months. If you build that kind of environment, people stay, they collaborate across boundaries, and they bring their friends.

And beyond the lab, I think doing open research, publishing, sharing code and models, connects you to the wider community. The field moves forward because many groups build on each other. A lab that only takes and never gives back eventually becomes isolated. So for me, research isn't just what we do. It's how we build a community, inside the company and outside of it.

r001.rationale: The response calls research “the glue” and says the research agenda itself brings people together at AMI Labs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think research is really the glue at AMI Labs, more than any org chart or product roadmap. When Yann and I started thinking about what this place should look like, one thing we kept coming back to was that the people we wanted to work with weren't going to join because of a title or a comp package. They'd join because there was a specific scientific question they couldn't stop thinking about, and they believed this was the place where they could actually chase it.

So research becomes the shared language. You have people coming from very different backgrounds — some from academia, some from industry labs, some who've spent years on vision, others on world models or planning or robotics. What lets them talk to each other is a common set of open problems. When we say we care about world models, about systems that learn from observation rather than just from text, about representation learning that isn't purely generative, that's not a slogan. It's a set of concrete bets that people can argue about, run experiments against, and build on top of each other's results.

And honestly, I think the arguing part is important. In a healthy research culture, people disagree a lot. The thing that keeps disagreement productive instead of corrosive is that everyone is oriented toward the same long-term question. You can fight about the method and still be on the same team about the goal.

The other piece is openness. Part of what I learned at NYU and before that at FAIR is that when you publish, when you release code and models, you're not just contributing to the field, you're recruiting. The next generation of people who care about these problems find you through the work. So research isn't only how we bring the current team together, it's how we find the people who should be here next.

I'd also say we try to keep the distance between research and engineering very small. At a lot of places there's a research org and a product org and a wall between them. We're trying hard not to build that wall. The people training the models should be the same people arguing about what the models should be. That's hard to maintain as you grow, but I think it's the thing that makes a lab feel like a lab rather than a company that happens to employ some researchers.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls research “the glue” at AMI Labs and explains that shared scientific questions and commitment to pursuing them bring people together.

astra-6.text:
I think research gives people a shared question to work on. You can bring together people with very different backgrounds, but that alone doesn’t make a team. The connection happens when you’re trying to understand the same problem—when you run an experiment, get a surprising result, and have to figure out together what it means.

That’s the role I see research playing at AMI Labs: creating a common purpose while leaving room for disagreement. You don’t need everyone to have the same intuition. You want people to challenge one another’s assumptions, and then have a way to test those ideas. Over time, that process builds both shared understanding and trust.

r001.rationale: The response says research brings people together through a shared problem, experiments, interpreting results, and testing ideas—describing the pursuit of sound research as their common purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research can give people a shared question to work on. People may come in with different backgrounds and different intuitions, but when you’re trying to understand the same problem, those differences become useful. You can challenge each other’s assumptions and learn from one another.

That’s the role I’d like research to play at AMI Labs: bringing people together through the work itself. It doesn’t mean everyone has to agree. You want people to feel comfortable disagreeing, testing ideas, and changing their minds. Over time, that process builds both understanding and trust.

r001.rationale: The response says research brings people together through a shared question and collaborative work, but does not identify the pursuit of doing research well as the underlying force.
